description: The DOJ has charged 36+ people with federal conspiracy for protesting ICE — using the same Civil War statute once reserved for the Proud Boys. Treasure Thoreson arrested in pajamas. Jac Archer convicted in Spokane. Up to 6 years in federal prison for blocking a deportation van.

faqs.answer: More than three dozen people have been charged under 18 USC 372 (conspiracy to impede an officer) in at least 10 cases. An additional ~50 people have been indicted on conspiracy charges under other statutes in Michigan, Texas, and Minnesota.
faqs.question: How many people has the DOJ charged with conspiracy for protesting ICE?

faqs.answer: Conspiracy to impede or injure an officer (18 USC 372) carries up to 6 years in federal prison. The DOJ's Pam Bondi memo directs prosecutors to charge protesters with 'the highest provable offense available under the law.'
faqs.question: What sentence do these charges carry?

faqs.answer: A special education teacher in Minneapolis arrested by Homeland Security agents at her home in June 2026. She was one of 15 people charged with conspiracy for blockading the Whipple Federal Building during ICE enforcement operations in Minnesota.
faqs.question: Who is Treasure Thoreson?

faqs.answer: Nine people were charged with conspiracy after a protest blocking an ICE detention van. Six pleaded guilty. Three went to trial. Jac Archer, policy director at Spokane Community Against Racism, was convicted. The acting U.S. attorney, Richard Barker, resigned rather than sign the original indictment.
faqs.question: What happened with the Spokane case?

keywords: Pam Bondi memo highest provable offense
leadParagraph: The DOJ has charged more than three dozen people with federal conspiracy for protesting immigration enforcement — using a Civil War-era statute that previously targeted far-right insurrectionists. Trump pardoned the Proud Boys. Now he's using the same law against the people who held hands in front of a deportation van.

mainImage.alt: Federal agents in tactical gear standing outside a government building in Minneapolis during immigration enforcement operations
mainImage.caption: Federal immigration agents stand guard outside a building in Minneapolis, Minnesota, January 10, 2026, during immigration enforcement operations that sparked widespread protests.

methodology: Reported using NPR's review of federal court records (August 3, 2026), interview with Treasure Thoreson, Jac Archer post-conviction reporting, Pam Bondi DOJ memo, Reuters reporting on internal DOJ email, Cornell Law statute text, and Spokane Public Radio original protest coverage.
title: The Conspiracy Charge: How the DOJ Is Turning Immigration Solidarity Into a Federal Crime
